vignette: Robert “Rob” Hayes is a 67-year-old widowed military medic who spent decades priding himself on staying steady in chaos. The accident that undid that certainty happened on a wet late afternoon as he was driving home. A car ahead of him spun across the lane and hit another vehicle hard enough to send metal scraping and glass bursting into the roadway. Rob stopped and moved toward the wreck by force of habit, already in medic mode, but the scene turned rapidly dangerous: leaking fuel, the sharp burnt smell of hot engine parts, and the heavy odor of alcohol on the breath of one of the injured drivers when Rob leaned in to assess him. Someone in the wreck was shouting. Tires screeched nearby. In later sessions he could begin the story, but as soon as he reached those moments he would lose the thread and stall out, looking frustrated and saying he could not explain it clearly from beginning to end. In the months afterward, the reminders that seized him were painfully specific. Passing a roadside crash, even a minor fender-bender, could pull up a burst of the scene. The smell of alcohol on a customer in a store or burnt food in a diner could hit him with a force that felt wildly out of proportion to the present moment. What frightened him was how immediate his body’s response was: his chest tightened, his heart kicked up, and he felt a jolt through him as if danger were happening again. Ordinary sounds started setting him off too; a dropped tray, a slammed car door, sudden brakes outside made him jump hard. He had come to notice those reminders everywhere, scanning parking lots and intersections for damaged cars and reacting to smells before he had consciously placed them. The memory itself did not feel like an ordinary recollection. At times it came with sound first—the screech of impact, the yelling at the scene—arriving in his head with such force that he would stop where he was and brace himself. After one of these episodes, he would keep hearing echoes of the crash in the world around him, so that a slammed car door or brakes outside no longer felt neutral. The memory left him primed to find pieces of the wreck everywhere for hours afterward. Just as unsettling, the memory could feel alien to him, as if it belonged to someone else and not to the man sitting in the room describing it. That estrangement fed what he had begun to believe about himself. He was convinced the event happened because of the way he acted at the scene, that he should have moved faster, judged better, done the right thing without hesitation. Having decided that he had failed in the one moment he should have been competent, he moved through later situations already braced, as if danger would find him again and expose the same weakness. That conviction made intersections, parking lots, and sudden noises feel charged before anything had actually happened. When the memory broke apart or felt unreal, he took that as further proof that he was weak and that he could no longer trust himself. The more he judged himself that way, the more insistently the accident seemed to return, as if his mind kept dragging him back to the scene to examine the evidence of his failure. Even the broken, unreal quality of it became part of what pulled it forward again. Those beliefs began organizing his days. Because he doubted his own judgment and was certain there was something wrong in the way his mind was handling the accident, Rob started monitoring his thoughts almost constantly for signs that he was “going crazy.” When the sense of danger surged that strongly, trying to control what he saw, thought about, and where he went felt like the only workable way to get through the day. Avoiding roads and pushing the images away made sense to him as basic self-protection. If an image of the wreck flashed up, he would immediately try to force it away. If he heard the remembered shouting in his head, he would clamp down harder, telling himself not to think about it. He also stopped driving whenever he could. As a military medic, even in a later-career role, vehicles and accident scenes had once been ordinary parts of his working life; now he arranged rides, altered routes, and avoided being a passenger unless there was no choice. At work and outside it, the effort to stay away from roads, collisions, and his own thoughts gradually narrowed his world. That effort did not settle things. The more Rob tried not to think about the crash, the more fragmented and ungraspable the memory became, and the more alien it felt when it broke through. Because he was continually checking his mind for danger signs, he noticed every intrusive sound and image the instant it appeared. Because he avoided driving, the sight of a wrecked car on the rare occasions he was on the road felt even more potent, almost unprocessed and new. His body stayed keyed up; being so jumpy made him even more vigilant for reminders, and that vigilance made the smell of alcohol, the scent of something burnt, or the glimpse of crumpled metal stand out immediately. Living at that pitch of alertness, almost any ambiguous cue could turn into a warning. The feeling of threat itself made the world seem crowded with signs that the crash was about to happen again. Because he no longer trusted his own judgment, things he might once have noticed and dismissed now snagged on him: the smell of alcohol on a stranger, the charred odor from a kitchen, a car stopped at an odd angle. His self-doubt made ordinary cues feel like ones he could not afford to overlook. Each episode seemed to confirm his private conclusion that he had failed in the moment that mattered and that he was not as strong as he had always believed. By the time he sought help, Rob was living in a shrinking orbit. He was embarrassed by how thoroughly his life had come to revolve around not being reminded, and ashamed that ordinary noises could make a former medic flinch. What finally brought him in was a recent incident in a hospital parking area when he caught the smell of alcohol on a passerby, heard a car horn and, for a moment, also heard again the shouting from the wreck; he froze and had to call for someone else to take over. More than anything, he is afraid that this reaction means he cannot trust his own mind or his judgment anymore. What he hopes, quietly, is not to become fearless, but to be able to tell the story all the way through and ride in a car without feeling as if the crash is waiting around the next corner.

violations.explanation: The vignette describes Rob’s negative beliefs about himself, but it does not clearly state in the same paragraph that these appraisals directly intensify or generate his sense of threat.
Although Rob interprets his fragmented memory negatively, no paragraph clearly states that his negative appraisals themselves cause the intrusive or fragmented memory to occur.

The vignette notes that Rob notices reminders everywhere and also holds negative beliefs, but it does not clearly link those appraisals as causing him to perceive or become more sensitive to triggers in the same paragraph.
The vignette shows triggers pulling up the trauma memory, but it does not clearly state that the memory itself leads to noticing, generating, or increasing triggers/reminders.
Rob’s body staying keyed up is described alongside vigilance and avoidance, but no paragraph clearly states that the sense of threat directly leads him to engage in maladaptive strategies.
The vignette describes jumpiness and vigilance making reminders stand out, but it does not clearly state that the felt threat itself leads to triggers/reminders in the same paragraph.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Threat: The vignette describes Rob’s negative beliefs about himself, but it does not clearly state in the same paragraph that these appraisals directly intensify or generate his sense of threat.
  e.g. "Having decided that she was permanently vulnerable, she walked into rooms already braced — the threat arrived with her before anything had happened."
  e.g. "The belief that she was a target — not unlucky, but chosen — meant that every unfamiliar face carried a weight of potential danger."
  e.g. "Her certainty that she couldn't protect herself made every new situation feel like a test she was already failing."
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: Although Rob interprets his fragmented memory negatively, no paragraph clearly states that his negative appraisals themselves cause the intrusive or fragmented memory to occur.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette notes that Rob notices reminders everywhere and also holds negative beliefs, but it does not clearly link those appraisals as causing him to perceive or become more sensitive to triggers in the same paragraph.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette shows triggers pulling up the trauma memory, but it does not clearly state that the memory itself leads to noticing, generating, or increasing triggers/reminders.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Maladaptive Strategies: Rob’s body staying keyed up is described alongside vigilance and avoidance, but no paragraph clearly states that the sense of threat directly leads him to engage in maladaptive strategies.
  e.g. "When the threat felt this close, planning her exit from every room she entered wasn't a symptom — it was just sensible."
  e.g. "She had found that checking the locks twice was the only thing that allowed her body to settle enough to sleep, so she checked them twice."
  e.g. "The only way to move through the world at that level of fear was to make it smaller — fewer places, fewer people, fewer chances for something to go wrong."
- Threat → Triggers: The vignette describes jumpiness and vigilance making reminders stand out, but it does not clearly state that the felt threat itself leads to triggers/reminders in the same paragraph.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
